n: Not many should rush to become teachers, James warns, because those who teach others are held to a stricter standard.
Everyone stumbles in many ways. Someone who never slips in speech would be a mature, complete person, able to control the rest of himself too.

f.g: Mature, complete—not flawless in every sense.

n: A small bit in a horse’s mouth steers the whole powerful animal. In the same way, controlling the tongue helps steer one’s whole life.

f.g: The metal mouthpiece of a bridle.

n: Huge ships pushed by strong winds are still turned by a small rudder wherever the pilot chooses. Small things can direct great ones.

f.g: The pilot wishes; list = to choose or desire.

n: The tongue is small but makes big claims and has big effects. One spark can set a whole forest ablaze.

f.g: How great a forest or woodland.

n: James uses strong images: careless or hateful speech is like fire fed by hell itself. It can corrupt a person and set the whole course of life burning.

f.g: Literally ‘the wheel of birth’—the whole cycle of human life.
Greek Gehenna, the burning valley outside Jerusalem used as an image of punishment.

n: Humans have tamed animals of every kind—wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and sea creatures.
Yet no one can fully tame the tongue by himself. It is restless and can spread poison like a snake. We need God’s help to govern our words.
We use the same tongue to praise God and to curse people—people made in God’s own image. That contradiction is the problem.
Blessing and cursing flowing from the same mouth should not be. Our speech should be consistent with our worship.
James uses nature to make his point: a spring doesn’t pour out sweet and bitter water from the same opening.
A fig tree can’t grow olives, and a grapevine can’t grow figs. What comes out of us reveals what we really are inside.
Who is truly wise? Let him show it by a good way of life and by actions done with the humility that wisdom brings.

f.g: In KJV English, conduct or way of life, not just talking.

n: If your heart is full of bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, don’t brag about being wise—that would be a lie against the truth.
That kind of “wisdom” doesn’t come from heaven. It is worldly, driven by natural appetites, and even demonic in origin.

f.g: Natural or unspiritual—governed by the physical self.

n: Where jealousy and rivalry rule, disorder and every kind of evil follow. Envy breaks families, wards, and communities apart.
Heavenly wisdom is described in a list worth memorizing: pure, peace-loving, gentle, open to reason, merciful, fruitful, fair, and sincere.

f.g: Willing to listen and be persuaded.

n: Peacemakers plant seeds in peace and harvest righteousness. Good outcomes grow out of a peaceful spirit.
